title: The Hottest Job at Big Law Firms Is Becoming Difficult to Fill
author: Roy Strom

dom.t: AI hiring: Implementation demand meets recruitment uncertainty

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s expectation of a changing skill mix and materially extends it with concrete hiring evidence: major firms are recruiting dedicated generative-AI professionals, encountering scarce expertise and considering law-school partnerships and peer coaching. It supports coordinated workforce and training adaptation, though it does not directly assess pyramid economics, junior displacement or pricing.
qs: LinkedIn displays at least 16 top law firms such as Latham & Watkins, Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, and Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman looking to hire more than 25 employees in total to build out their generative AI strategies or capabilities.

The bottleneck has some firms looking for alternatives, such as partnering with law schools to design “AI native lawyers,” or asking lawyers who’ve been early adopters of AI to coach colleagues through the change.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s adaptation argument with concrete evidence that firms are investing in multidisciplinary AI capability but face a scarce-talent bottleneck. Advertised roles, high salaries and training alternatives show that implementation depends on legal-technical expertise and organisational capacity, not merely access to AI tools, though the source does not assess pricing or staffing-model effects.
qs: LinkedIn displays at least 16 top law firms such as Latham & Watkins, Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, and Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman looking to hire more than 25 employees in total to build out their generative AI strategies or capabilities.
“The simplest truth is there just isn’t enough of this talent in the market,” said Josh Kubicki, a professor at Indiana University Maurer School of Law.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised, task-level augmentation framing and materially extends its organisational-complements argument by identifying scarce AI-leadership talent as a deployment bottleneck and documenting concrete alternatives: internal AI champions, legal-operations-led change management and law-school partnerships that combine AI fluency with lawyer verification and judgment.
qs: The bottleneck has some firms looking for alternatives, such as partnering with law schools to design “AI native lawyers,” or asking lawyers who’ve been early adopters of AI to coach colleagues through the change.
The class will pair today’s law students who are fluent in using AI, Kubicki said, with lawyers who are competent enough to know when it is wrong and what parts of the job can’t risk being automated.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source accepts the broader restructuring account and materially extends it with concrete hiring evidence: major firms are creating well-paid AI capability roles, encountering a scarce experienced-talent pool, and exploring law-school partnerships and peer coaching to develop AI-native skills. It supports the cluster’s competence and institutional-adaptation points, though it does not directly assess junior displacement or profession-wide headcount.
qs: LinkedIn displays at least 16 top law firms such as Latham & Watkins, Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, and Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman looking to hire more than 25 employees in total to build out their generative AI strategies or capabilities.

The bottleneck has some firms looking for alternatives, such as partnering with law schools to design “AI native lawyers,” or asking lawyers who’ve been early adopters of AI to coach colleagues through the change.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s augmentation-led, human-supervised model and materially develops its institutional-absorption argument by showing concrete capability-building strategies: legal-operations-led change management, internal lawyer champions, and task-level collaboration between AI-fluent students and experienced lawyers who verify outputs and identify work too risky to automate. Its adoption and efficiency figures remain reported usage and targets, not demonstrated market-wide outcomes.
qs: That operations team has led the firm on other change management initiatives, and AI is just the latest example.
The class will pair today’s law students who are fluent in using AI, Kubicki said, with lawyers who are competent enough to know when it is wrong and what parts of the job can’t risk being automated.

st.t: AI hiring: Implementation demand meets recruitment uncertainty
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: firms face strong demand and scarce supply for AI implementation talent while choosing between specialist recruitment and internal capability-building. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that advertised salaries, adoption rates and efficiency targets indicate intentions or usage rather than demonstrated value or employment effects.
qs: “The simplest truth is there just isn’t enough of this talent in the market,” said Josh Kubicki, a professor at Indiana University Maurer School of Law.
Barnes & Thornburg’s strategy is to build AI expertise in the lawyers who will deliver it to clients.

kp.k: AI strategy hiring encounters scarce talent and competing employers
kp.d: Strom reports LinkedIn postings from at least 16 top law firms seeking more than 25 employees to develop generative AI strategies or capabilities, with annual pay from $200,000 to more than $400,000. Firms prefer lawyers with at least 10 years of AI experience and demonstrated technology-adoption results. The article identifies insufficient qualified candidates and competition from corporate legal departments; Josh Kubicki characterises demand as exceeding supply.
qs: They want professionals, preferably lawyers, with at least 10 years of artificial intelligence experience who have proven results helping law firms adopt new technologies.

LinkedIn displays at least 16 top law firms such as Latham & Watkins, Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, and Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman looking to hire more than 25 employees in total to build out their generative AI strategies or capabilities.
“The simplest truth is there just isn’t enough of this talent in the market,” said Josh Kubicki, a professor at Indiana University Maurer School of Law. “Demand is running well ahead of supply.”

kp.k: Kirkland's platform investment intensifies AI capability building
kp.d: Strom presents Kirkland & Ellis’ planned $500 million investment in its own AI platform as increasing other firms’ sense of urgency. The plan includes employing hundreds of AI professionals; these are planned investments and staffing requirements, not reported completed deployments.
qs: Kirkland & Ellis’ plan to spend $500 million building its own AI platform has focused law firms on the urgency of building out their AI capabilities.
To less fanfare, plenty of other firms are building their AI bench.

kp.k: AI hiring creates specialised innovation and engineering leadership roles
kp.d: The reported openings span knowledge management, governance, legal innovation, data services and engineering. Latham seeks innovation professionals, most with law degrees, earning $295,000–$400,000. Gibson Dunn offers up to $380,000 for two director roles and seeks a law degree or MBA, 15 years of AI, machine-learning or legal-technology experience, and prior legal-industry work. Pillsbury’s technical director would build a team delivering AI solutions, indicating demand for both legal expertise and technical implementation capabilities.
qs: It is looking to employ associate directors of AI for knowledge management, governance, and AI innovation.
These professionals, most of whom should have law degrees, will earn between $295,000 and $400,000.
The firm wants a professional with a law degree or MBA with 15 years of AI, machine learning, or legal technology experience who has previously worked in the legal industry.
The person with a more technical skillset will build a team of data scientists and legal operations engineers delivering “product-ready” AI solutions.

kp.k: Chart documents high salary ceilings across professional roles
kp.d: The accompanying LinkedIn-based chart contains 18 postings across 10 firms, distinct from the article’s broader hiring count. Its figures are posting salary ceilings, ranging from $300,000 to $440,000, rather than actual compensation paid. Pillsbury’s Director, Data Science & AI Engineering has the highest ceiling at $440,000, followed by Covington & Burling’s Director of Applied AI at $438,000. The document characterises most listed positions as non-lawyer professional roles rather than attorney positions.
qs: Salaries are the **High End Salary** of each posting.
| Pillsbury | Director, Data Science & AI Engineering | $440,000 |
| Covington & Burling | Director of Applied AI | $438,000 |
Most titles are **non-lawyer professional roles** (director/senior-manager grade), not attorney positions.

kp.k: Meta specifies prospective agent-driven contracting efficiency targets
kp.d: Strom says comparable corporate legal-department roles typically pay less but sometimes specify more concrete objectives. Meta seeks a director of commercial legal AI to implement agents targeting 20%–30% efficiency gains in commercial contracting within one year. The role offers up to $286,000 annually plus bonus and equity. These gains are hiring objectives, not measured outcomes.
qs: Similar jobs offered by law departments typically don’t pay as much. But they sometimes advertise more concrete objectives.

Meta’s legal department, for instance, wants a director of commercial legal AI to implement AI agents that can deliver, in one year, 20% to 30% efficiency gains in the company’s commercial contracting process.
The job pays up to $286,000 a year and offers a bonus and equity.

kp.k: Barnes builds lawyer-led adoption instead of recruiting AI directors
kp.d: Barnes & Thornburg named 38 early-adopter lawyers as AI Practice Champions to share expertise with peers. Managing partner Andrew Detherage attributes its change-management capacity to a decade-long legal-operations investment. The article reports nearly 90% of attorneys actively using AI and more than 1,000 using Harvey. Detherage says the firm is not seeking an AI director of the kind competitors want, citing intense competition, including from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
qs: The firm this week named 38 “AI Practice Champions,” who are early adopters of the technology and will disseminate what they’ve learned to their peers.
The firm has benefited from a decade-long investment in legal operations, the firm’s managing partner, Andrew Detherage, said.
Adoption is picking up, with nearly 90% of the firm’s attorneys actively using AI, and more than 1,000 using Harvey.
“If you have the skills you just described, Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are hiring everybody they can possibly hire,” Detherage said. “Those are really, really marketable skills.”

kp.k: Ice Miller links legal education to task-level AI augmentation
kp.d: Ice Miller is taking a longer-term talent-development approach through a class with Indiana law professor Kubicki: students will study lawyers’ discrete tasks and design AI augmentation. Chief managing partner Joshua Christie says the firm is not currently hiring AI directors; its existing innovation team works with early adopters on deployment. He frames the partnership as an investment in changing lawyer formation and firm operations, rather than reporting demonstrated educational or productivity outcomes.
qs: The law firm has partnered with Kubicki, the Indiana law professor, to sponsor a class where students will study how Ice Miller lawyers handle discrete tasks and design ways they can be augmented by AI.
Joshua Christie, chief managing partner of Ice Miller, said his firm isn’t hiring AI directors at the moment.
His existing innovation team is working with early adopters to deploy AI throughout the firm.
“We really need to understand what the AI native lawyer looks like and how we build them.”

kp.k: AI fluency must be paired with substantive legal competence
kp.d: Kubicki distinguishes students’ AI fluency from experienced lawyers’ competence to recognise incorrect outputs and identify work that cannot safely be automated. The planned class pairs these capabilities. His warning that firms will discover they needed competence rather than merely fluency is a prospective judgment, not an empirical finding about hiring outcomes.
qs: The class will pair today’s law students who are fluent in using AI, Kubicki said, with lawyers who are competent enough to know when it is wrong and what parts of the job can’t risk being automated.
“Firms are hiring hard for fluency and they are going to discover they needed competence,” he said.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is creating demand for highly paid legal-innovation professionals, but scarcity and competition are encouraging firms to develop internal expertise; efficiency gains and changes in lawyer education are also anticipated.
pts.d: Roy Strom reports that Big Law firms are expanding recruitment for professionals who can build generative-AI capabilities and lead adoption, with advertised compensation ranging from $200,000 to more than $400,000. He characterizes experienced talent as scarce and sought by both firms and corporate legal departments. Josh Kubicki explicitly claims demand exceeds supply. Strom also says Kirkland & Ellis’ planned $500 million AI-platform investment, including hiring hundreds of AI professionals, has increased other firms’ sense of urgency. Andrew Detherage describes competition from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI for the same skills. As alternatives to external recruitment, Strom describes internal coaching and law-school partnerships. At Barnes & Thornburg, Detherage reports that an established legal-operations team supports adoption, with nearly 90% of attorneys actively using AI and more than 1,000 using Harvey. Meta’s legal-department posting specifies a prospective objective—not an achieved result—of using AI agents to deliver 20%–30% efficiency gains in commercial contracting within one year. Kubicki argues that AI fluency alone is insufficient: lawyers need substantive competence to recognize errors and identify tasks that cannot safely be automated. Ice Miller’s Joshua Christie presents its law-school partnership as an investment in changing lawyer education and firm operations and developing an 'AI native lawyer.'

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on LinkedIn job postings, reported investment and training initiatives, and interviews with a law professor and managing partners; it does not provide measured AI efficiency results.
pts.d: Strom’s recruitment evidence is a LinkedIn snapshot identifying at least 16 top firms seeking more than 25 employees. Specific postings include Latham roles paying $295,000–$400,000, Gibson Dunn director positions paying up to $380,000, Pillsbury’s data-science and AI-engineering director paying up to $440,000, and Covington’s applied-AI director paying up to $438,000. The accompanying chart contains 18 postings from 10 firms, with high-end advertised salaries of $300,000–$440,000; these are posting maxima, not actual earnings or the full article-wide hiring count. Experience requirements include Gibson Dunn’s request for 15 years in AI, machine learning, or legal technology plus prior legal-industry work. Talent scarcity is supported by Kubicki’s and Detherage’s interview assessments and evidence of competing vacancies, rather than a quantified talent-supply or vacancy-duration study. Barnes & Thornburg’s 38 AI Practice Champions, decade-long legal-operations investment, and reported adoption levels provide a firm-specific example of internal development. Ice Miller’s sponsored class and existing innovation-team activity provide another implementation example. Meta’s percentage target comes from a job advertisement, not an outcome evaluation. The source offers no benchmark or measured productivity evidence establishing that the proposed contracting gains or education benefits have occurred.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Recruitment and adoption claims concern the reporting period; Meta has a one-year target, while internal talent development and education changes have no specified completion date.
pts.d: The supplied document labels the article 2026. Strom describes hiring needs and vacancies as current, but gives no precise date for the LinkedIn snapshot. The search for candidates with at least a decade of relevant experience is a qualification for the desired talent, not a forecast horizon; the specific Gibson Dunn requirement also allows experience in machine learning or legal technology. Kirkland’s $500 million platform expenditure and employment of hundreds are described as a plan, without a completion date. Meta’s contracting-efficiency objective is explicitly to be delivered in one year and depends on implementing AI agents. Barnes & Thornburg’s champion appointments occurred 'this week,' while its supporting legal-operations investment extends over a decade; its adoption figures describe current usage rather than a future projection. Barnes & Thornburg and Ice Miller are not recruiting AI directors at the time described, not necessarily rejecting such hiring permanently. Ice Miller’s education initiative is explicitly longer-term. Kubicki conditions successful augmentation on combining students’ AI fluency with experienced lawyers’ ability to check correctness and recognize unacceptable automation risks; his warning about firms discovering the need for competence has no fixed deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported changes primarily affect large law firms, specialist professional staff, practicing lawyers, law students, and corporate legal departments.
pts.d: Large firms face competition for experienced AI-adoption leaders and are building teams across data science, AI engineering, knowledge management, governance, legal innovation and training. The chart mainly concerns director and senior-manager professional roles rather than attorney positions, although several employers prefer or require legal qualifications. Candidates with combined technical, legal-industry and change-management experience gain access to high advertised salaries and competing employers. Corporate legal departments are competing buyers of talent, distinct from law-firm providers: Meta, Honeywell, Broadcom and SharkNinja are named. Strom says their comparable jobs typically pay less, while Meta additionally offers bonus and equity and a specific commercial-contracting objective. Practicing lawyers at Barnes & Thornburg become both AI users and peer coaches; legal-operations staff support organizational change. At Ice Miller, existing lawyers contribute judgment about correctness and automation risk, while students help design task-level augmentation and develop new professional capabilities. Clients are contemplated as recipients of services from AI-capable lawyers, but the source provides no measured client-price, service-quality or access-to-justice effects and makes no concrete prediction of lawyer job losses.
